# Population projections in the EU

Data extracted in April 2026 

Planned update date: April 2027 

## Highlights

The EU population is projected to increase from 451.8 million in 2025 and peak at 453.3 million in 2029 (+0.3%), then gradually decrease to 445.0 million in 2050 and to 398.8 million in 2100. 

Median age of the EU population expected to increase by 6.6 years between 2025 and 2100. 

Proportion of people aged 65 years or over is projected to reach a third of total population in 2100. 

This article focuses on projected developments of the population size and structure for all European Union (EU) Member States and 3 of the 4 European Free Trade Association (EFTA) countries, covering the period 2025 to 2100, based on the latest EUROPOP2025 population projections released by Eurostat on 16 April 2026. The size and composition of a population changes over time as a function of 3 demographic events: births, deaths and migratory flows. The main outcome of the current levels of fertility and mortality in the EU is a progressive ageing of the population. This is an ongoing demographic process and its consequences are analysed by policymakers from social, economic and labour-related perspectives. EUROPOP2025 are deterministic projections, or 'what-if' population projections, based on assumptions formulated on a future course of fertility, mortality and migration. The scenario is that of partial convergence among the countries included in EUROPOP2025 in fertility, mortality and migration developments. The methodology used in this projection round builds heavily upon the previous projections exercises and their methodological reports are useful complements. 

## Projected changes in population totals

EUROPOP2025, the latest population projections released by Eurostat on 16 April 2025, provide the baseline projections for population developments from 2025 to 2100 for 30 European countries: all of the EU countries and 3 EFTA countries (Iceland, Norway and Switzerland), using data for population on 1 January 2025 as a starting point. Eurostat's population projections result from the application of a set of assumptions on future developments for fertility, mortality and net migration. The projections should not be considered as forecasts, as they show what would happen to the resulting population structure if the set of assumptions are held constant over the entire time horizon under consideration; in other words, the projections are 'what-if' scenarios that track population developments under a set of assumptions. As these projections are made over a relatively long time horizon, statements about the likely future developments of the EU's population should be treated with caution and interpreted as only one of a range of possible demographic developments. The additional available projection scenarios published show the wide range of possible outcomes under different assumptions. This article presents the main results of the baseline projections and includes the most recent official statistics available at the time of writing this article; for a more detailed presentation of the latest published data for the reference year 2024, please refer to the article on population and population change statistics. 

EU population projected to grow very slightly until 2029, followed by an increasingly steep decline until the end of the century 

The EU population is projected to slightly increase from 451.8 million in 2025 to 453.3 million in 2029 (+0.3%), then gradually decrease to 445.0 million in 2050 and then accelerate its decline to 398.8 million in 2100, with an overall decrease of 53.0 million (-11.7%) from 2025 to 2100 (see Figure 1). 

Figure 1

In 2100, Germany will remain the most populous EU country followed by France and Spain 

Between individual countries, the changes in the projected population structure vary considerably, both in terms of when the highest level of population will be reached and the direction and magnitude of change. In terms of total population, Germany will remain the largest country, despite a projected decline from 83.6 million in 2025 to 74.7 in 2100. It is followed by France with a projected total of 67.2 million in 2100 (down from 68.9 million in 2025) and Spain, which is projected to grow from 49.1 million to 49.8 million. Despite being projected to grow substantially, Malta and Luxembourg are projected to remain the least populous countries, with both projected populations remaining under 1 million. Figure 1 shows the trajectory of projected populations for all countries and aggregates between 2025 and 2100. Figure 2 shows the increase in % from 2025 to selected time periods, and for different age groups. In both figures, individual countries can be selected in the drop-down menu. An increase in the number of inhabitants is projected for 9 EU countries and for all 3 EFTA countries considered here. Population numbers are projected to rise by more than 25.0% until 2100 in 2 countries: Luxembourg (+36.4%), and Malta (+26.0%). Of the remaining countries, growth between 10.0% - 20% is projected for Sweden and Ireland. 

By contrast, the total population is projected to fall between 2025 and 2100 in 18 EU countries. Among these, there will be a relatively modest decline in the total number of people living in France and Austria, where the population is projected to contract by less than 5%. Declines of about 10% of the total population are projected for Germany, Slovenia, Finland and Czechia. The largest declines – with the total number of inhabitants between 2025 and 2100 falling by more than 30.0% – are projected for Greece (-30.1%), Poland (-31.6%), Lithuania (-33.4%) and Latvia (-33.9%). 

Figure 2

## Impact of births, deaths and migration on population change

At EU level, over the entire period between 2025 and 2100, a higher number of deaths than live births is projected, resulting in a continuous negative natural change (the difference between births and deaths). Figure 3 shows the projected developments for each vital event, as well as net migration, with the widest gap between the numbers of deaths and births projected for the decade from 2055 to 2064, exceeding 2.5 million persons. At country level, Eurostat's projections indicate that there will be considerable differences in natural population changes developments during the period from 2025 to 2100, with: 

- An initial positive natural population change, but an overall negative balance over the projections' horizon – for 6 EU countries (Sweden, Luxembourg, Ireland, Cyprus, Malta, Denmark) and the 3 EFTA countries;
- Negative natural change in each year of the projections' horizon – for the remaining EU countries.

Figure 3

Migratory patterns – immigration and emigration – also have an impact on the total population as well as the population age structures, resulting from either positive net migration (more people arriving in a country than leaving it) or negative net migration (more people leaving a country than arriving), and how both migration flows are distributed over the age groups. In the EUROPOP2025 projections, high and persistent positive net migration is the only factor contributing to population growth for those countries that are projected to grow over the time period between 2025 to 2100. In those EU countries which are characterised by positive net migration, it is possible that the process of population ageing may be slowed down, as migrant populations often have a high share of working-age persons. However, some countries have sizeable net immigration of pension-aged persons, such that positive net migration can also contribute to ageing. Also with negative net migration, the ageing process may be accelerated, as those leaving the country may also be relatively young, thereby reducing the number of working-age persons in the population, while also reducing the fertility rate. Table 1 shows the cumulative contributions of natural population change and net migration to the total population change in the EU and for all EU countries until 2100. Over the period 2025 to 2100, Eurostat's projections suggest that there will be 253.0 million births and 409.8 million deaths in the EU, equivalent to a rounded net reduction of 156.7 million people due to natural changes in the population. The cumulated net migration is projected to contribute an increase of 103.7 million persons, resulting in an overall decrease of 53.0 million people in the total EU population. 

Table 1: Demographic balances, 1 January 2025-2100 Source: Eurostat (proj_25ndbi)

## Projected changes in population composition

The Eurostat baseline scenario projects that the current pattern of population ageing in the EU is likely to continue until 2100, with both the size and the proportion of older persons in the total population increasing. Various demographic indicators are used to analyse the shift in age distribution towards older ages, including: 

- the median age;
- the proportion of population in each of the main demographic age groups - children (defined here as those aged 0-14 years), the working-age population (15-64 years) and the elderly population (65 years and over); and,
- age-dependency ratios - such as the young-age dependency ratio, the old-age dependency ratio or total-age dependency ratio.

Figure 4 shows that during the period 2025 to 2100, the median age of the EU population is projected to increase by 6.6 years to reach 51.5 years in 2100. All countries are expected to experience an increase in the median ages of their population. Malta, Cyprus, Ireland, Luxembourg, Lithuania and Poland are projected to see their median ages rising by more than 10 years. The smallest increases below 6 years are projected for Bulgaria, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Greece, Slovenia and Czechia. Overall, the youngest populations are projected to be Bulgaria, the Netherlands, and Germany, with median ages just below 50 years. On the other side of the spectrum, projections indicate that by the end of the century, the median age is likely to rise above 53.0 years in 7 countries: Lithuania, Malta, Cyprus, Italy, Spain, Portugal, and Poland. The exact projected median ages for all countries and specific time periods can be selected and read off the interactive Figure 4. 

Figure 4

Share of people aged 65 and over in the EU projected to increase to a third of total population until 2100 

The projected relative and absolute sizes of different age groups follow contrasting developments (see Figure 5). The proportion of young people (0-19 years old) in the EU total population is projected to decline in both relative and absolute terms, from a share of 19.8% (89.5 million) at the beginning of 2025 to 16.7% (66.6 million) in 2100. The share of working-age population (20-64 years old) in the EU total population is projected to decrease from 58.3% (263.2 million) at the beginning of 2025 to 49.7% (198.4 million) in 2100, representing an overall reduction of 64.9 million persons. The proportion of elderly (65 years and over) in the EU total population is projected to increase from 21.9% (99.0 million) at the beginning of 2025 to 33.6% (133.8 million) in 2100. As such, the share of elderly persons is projected to rise by +11.7 percentage points (pp), corresponding to additional 34.8 million persons by 2100. With the overall EU population declining by 2100, this is the only main demographic age group that is projected to grow considerably, both in relative and absolute terms, indicating an acceleration of population ageing. 

Figure 5
